description: Team 8 from Miva Open University, Abuja. We’re building Miva FireLens, an interactive platform that merges NASA MODIS and VIIRS fire data to help responders spot and track wildfires faster. I’m Victor, product designer with 10 years in tech; we also have a software engineer building the prototype. Join us to ship real impact with NASA data. Looking for: GIS/remote sensing or data science (Python, NASA FIRMS), and map/front-end dev skills.
summary:
Miva FireLens: Learn from Yesterday. Prepare for Tomorrow.

Miva FireLens is a Nigeria-focused platform developed to make historical satellite fire data easier to explore, understand and interpret. Using NASA's open FIRMS active-fire observations from MODIS and VIIRS instruments, FireLens allows users to explore historical fire activity across Nigerian states, identify recurring seasonal patterns and compare activity across different years.

The project addresses a key challenge in historical fire monitoring: MODIS and VIIRS have different spatial resolutions and detection capabilities, making their raw fire counts difficult to compare directly. FireLens addresses this challenge by distinguishing raw satellite observations from harmonized estimates intended to improve historical comparability.

By transforming complex satellite observations into accessible maps, trends and seasonal summaries, FireLens aims to support environmental awareness, historical analysis and better-informed fire preparedness. Its importance lies in helping decision-makers learn from previous fire patterns and make more informed plans for future fire seasons.
details:
Miva FireLens

Miva FireLens is a web-based platform designed to make historical satellite fire observations across Nigeria easier to explore, analyse and understand.

The platform uses NASA's open Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS) data, particularly active-fire observations from the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) and Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS). Users can explore fire activity across Nigerian states, examine historical trends, identify recurring seasonal patterns and compare activity across different years through interactive maps, visualisations and summaries.

One of the key challenges addressed by FireLens is the difference between MODIS and VIIRS detection capabilities. MODIS provides a longer historical record, while VIIRS offers finer spatial resolution and can detect smaller thermal signals. Directly combining their raw detection counts can therefore produce misleading historical comparisons. FireLens addresses this issue by distinguishing raw observations from harmonized estimates intended to improve comparability across the sensor transition.

The platform offers several benefits. It makes complex satellite information more accessible, helps users investigate historical fire hotspots, supports seasonal comparisons and provides useful context for environmental monitoring and preparedness planning.

Its intended impact is to help environmental planners, researchers and relevant decision-makers use historical evidence to make better-informed decisions before and during recurring fire seasons. FireLens does not predict or prevent fires; it supports understanding and preparedness through historical data exploration.

The project creatively combines freely available NASA Earth observation data with interactive data visualisation and a Nigeria-focused user experience. Rather than simply displaying satellite detections, it focuses on explaining what the observations mean, how they change over time and why differences between satellite instruments matter.

During development, the team considered data reliability, satellite resolution, historical coverage, sensor differences, usability, geographical relevance and the limitations of satellite observations. These considerations help ensure that users interpret the information responsibly.
